name: Kinnersley Photon Rocket
description: The field of a point mass that accelerates by shining light unevenly, found by William Kinnersley in 1969. Its mass and its acceleration are arbitrary functions of retarded time, the light is null dust that streams out brightest behind it, and no gravitational waves reach infinity.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ and $G$ explicit, and the Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$. The mass function is $m = GM/c^2$, a length.
history: A body that shines more light out of one side than the other is pushed the opposite way, a rocket whose exhaust is light [bonnor1994]. William Kinnersley wrote down its gravitational field in 1969, "a metric of the Kerr-Schild type" that "contains four arbitrary functions of time" [kinnersley1969]. He called it "a generalization of Vaidya's shining-star metric" that "permits arbitrary acceleration of the source" [kinnersley1969, vaidya1951]. The four functions are the mass $m$ of the rocket and the three components of its acceleration [carlip2000]. With $m = 0$ the metric is Minkowski's in Ezra Newman and T. W. J. Unti's coordinates of 1963 for an arbitrary timelike world line [newman1963, podolsky2011]. The retarded time $u$ is the proper time along the world line and labels its future light cones, $r$ is an affine parameter along their rays, and the mass adds the single term $(2m/r)\,c^2du^2$, where $m = GM/c^2$ [podolsky2011].¶The Ricci tensor has a single component, the energy of pure radiation, matter of zero rest mass that streams out of $r = 0$ along the rays and thins as $1/r^2$ [podolsky2008]. For a rocket on a straight line with acceleration $\alpha(u)$, the density of that radiation at the angle $\theta$ from the direction opposite to the acceleration is proportional to $3\alpha m\cos\theta - dm/d(cu)$ [podolsky2008]. The light is brightest straight behind the rocket and faintest straight ahead, and the recoil accelerates it [bonnor1994, podolsky2008]. The density stays positive in every direction only when $dm/d(cu) < -3|\alpha m|$: to keep accelerating, the rocket must keep losing mass [podolsky2008]. With $\alpha = 0$ the light leaves evenly in all directions and the metric is Vaidya's, and with $m$ constant as well it is Schwarzschild's [podolsky2008]. The name "photon rocket" was in the literature by the time Thibault Damour took up the solution in 1995 [damour1995].¶An accelerated mass ought to send out gravitational waves, and this one sends none to infinity [damour1995]. William Bonnor examined the solution in 1994, found "no sign of emission of gravitational radiation", and gave its Killing vectors and some of its curvature invariants [bonnor1994]. Damour called the puzzle Bonnor's paradox [damour1995]. To resolve it he took a point mass in Minkowski space that emits null fluid anisotropically and recoils, and computed the linearized retarded waves of the mass and of its photons together [damour1995]. Where the anisotropy is purely dipolar, as in Kinnersley's solution, the wave amplitude of the photons "exactly cancels the usual $1/r$ gravitational wave amplitude generated by the accelerated motion of the rocket" [damour1995]. A rocket whose light has a quadrupole or any higher multipole, $\ell \geq 2$, does send gravitational waves to infinity [damour1995].¶Bonnor's second family of photon rockets, of 1996, lets the photons leave with an almost arbitrary distribution over the angles, and is of Petrov type II where Kinnersley's is of type D [bonnor1996, podolsky2008]. Kinnersley's rocket belongs to the family of Robinson and Trautman, and Sergio Dain, Osvaldo Moreschi, and Reinaldo Gleiser used that in 1996 to tell apart, far from the rocket, the energy its light carries off from any that gravitational waves carry off, the radiation of the Ricci tensor and of the Weyl tensor [dain1996, robinson1962]. Among the axisymmetric members of that family filled with pure radiation, Kinnersley's rocket is the only one that sends out no gravitational waves, a result U. von der Gönna and Dietrich Kramer reached in 1998 in Bondi-Sachs coordinates [vondergonna1998]. F. H. J. Cornish dropped the axis in 2000: a Robinson-Trautman spacetime with pure radiation sends out no gravitational waves, which is to say its news function vanishes, exactly when it is one of Kinnersley's rockets [cornish2000, podolsky2008].¶How fast does the pull of a moving mass travel? Steven Carlip put the question to the rocket in 2000, since Einstein's equations let a mass accelerate only when the energy responsible for the acceleration is included [carlip2000]. A test particle near the rocket falls almost toward where the rocket is now: toward its retarded position extrapolated quadratically to the present, up to small nonlinear terms and corrections of higher order in the velocity [carlip2000]. The aberration expected of a field that travels at the speed of light is "almost exactly canceled by velocity-dependent interactions" [carlip2000].¶The rocket flies in any number of dimensions: Metin Gürses and Özgür Sarıoğlu wrote a class of Kerr-Schild metrics that holds it in 2002, and Jiří Podolský and Marcello Ortaggio found the class independently in 2006 among the Robinson-Trautman spacetimes [gurses2002, podolsky2006, podolsky2011]. With a cosmological constant, which Podolský added in 2008, it flies through de Sitter or anti-de Sitter space [podolsky2008]. Its whole axis is regular, where the black holes of the C-metric, the other accelerating spacetime of type D in the family, need a cosmic string or a strut along theirs [podolsky2008]. In 2011 Podolský sent rockets along a straight line and around a circle and worked out their radiation patterns and their loss of mass [podolsky2011]. Set spinning, the rocket is Peter Hogan and Dirk Puetzfeld's field of 2020, which is Kerr's solution when the acceleration vanishes and Kinnersley's when the rotation does [hogan2020].

related.text: The rocket with its engine off and its lamp still on. With $\alpha = 0$ the light leaves evenly in all directions and the metric is Vaidya's shining star [podolsky2008].
The rocket gone dark. With $\alpha = 0$ and $m$ constant no light leaves, and the metric is Schwarzschild's in retarded time [podolsky2008].
The rocket's wave fronts are Robinson and Trautman's, round spheres that expand without shear or twist, with pure radiation let into their vacuum [dain1996].

The other accelerating spacetime of type D among Robinson and Trautman's. Its black holes are pulled along by a cosmic string or pushed by a strut, and the rocket pushes itself with light [podolsky2008].
Light as the source again, here a steady beam of parallel rays with no rocket to push. William Bonnor found its exact field in 1969 [bonnor1969light].

coordinates.name: Rectilinear

parameters.description: Mass function of retarded time, the length $GM(u)/c^2$; the radiation has positive density in every direction where $\partial_u m \le -3|\alpha|m$
Proper acceleration of the rocket over $c^2$, an inverse length, positive toward $\theta = \pi$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ for a rocket that moves along a line, with the retarded time $u$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ an affine length along the rays, and $\theta$ the angle of a ray in the rocket's rest frame, measured from the direction opposite to its acceleration. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, so $\partial_u m = c^{-1}dm/du$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{\alpha^3\,r^5\sin^2\theta\cos\theta + 2\alpha^2\,m\,r^3\sin^2\theta - 2\alpha^2\,r^4\sin^2\theta + 2\alpha^2\,r^4 - \alpha\,r^3\cos\theta - 2m^2 + m\,r - r^4\,\partial_u\alpha\,\cos\theta - r^2\,\partial_u m}{r^3}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{2m - 2\alpha\,r^2\cos\theta}{r^2}\dot{u}\dot{r} + 2\alpha\left(\alpha\,r^2\cos\theta + 2m\right)\sin\theta\,\dot{u}\dot{\theta} + \left(\alpha\,r^2\cos\theta + 2m - r\right)\dot{\theta}^2 + \left(\alpha\,r^2\cos\theta + 2m - r\right)\sin^2\theta\,\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

parameters.description: Mass function of retarded time, the length $GM(u)/c^2$
Component of the rocket's four-velocity over $c$ along the first axis of the background inertial frame, the polar axis $\theta = 0$
Component of the rocket's four-velocity over $c$ along the second axis, $\theta = \pi/2$ and $\phi = 0$
Component of the rocket's four-velocity over $c$ along the third axis, $\theta = \pi/2$ and $\phi = \pi/2$

parameters.symbol: p = \sqrt{1 + U_1^2 + U_2^2 + U_3^2} - U_1\cos\theta - U_2\sin\theta\cos\phi - U_3\sin\theta\sin\phi
parameters.description: Dimensionless function fixing the metric $r^2p^{-2}(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\,d\phi^2)$ of each wave front, a round sphere of radius $r$; its first term is the time component of the four-velocity over $c$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(u, r, \theta, \phi)$ for a rocket in arbitrary motion, with the retarded time $u$ carrying dimensions of time, $r$ an affine length along the rays, and $\theta$ and $\phi$ the polar angles of a ray's direction in the inertial frame of the flat background. We take components in the chart $x^0 = cu$, so $\partial_u p = c^{-1}\partial p/\partial u$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{u}$ means $d(cu)/d\lambda$.

nonzero.value: \dfrac{3r^4\left(\partial_u p\right)^2 - p\,r^4\,\partial_u^2 p - p\,r^3\,\partial_u p - p^2\,r^2\,\partial_u m + p^2\,m\,r - 2p^2\,m^2}{p^2\,r^3}

geodesics: \ddot{r} + \dfrac{3r^4\left(\partial_u p\right)^2 - p\,r^4\,\partial_u^2 p - p\,r^3\,\partial_u p - p^2\,r^2\,\partial_u m + p^2\,m\,r - 2p^2\,m^2}{p^2\,r^3}\dot{u}^2 + \dfrac{2p\,m - 2r^2\,\partial_u p}{p\,r^2}\dot{u}\dot{r} + \dfrac{2r\left(\partial_\theta p\,\partial_u p - p\,\partial_u\partial_\theta p\right)}{p^2}\dot{u}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2r\left(\partial_\phi p\,\partial_u p - p\,\partial_u\partial_\phi p\right)}{p^2}\dot{u}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{2p\,m - p\,r + r^2\,\partial_u p}{p^3}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{\left(2p\,m - p\,r + r^2\,\partial_u p\right)\sin^2\theta}{p^3}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{\theta} + \dfrac{\partial_\theta p\,\partial_u p - p\,\partial_u\partial_\theta p}{r}\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{2\partial_u p}{p}\dot{u}\dot{\theta} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\theta} - \dfrac{\partial_\theta p}{p}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{2\partial_\phi p}{p}\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{\left(\partial_\theta p\,\sin\theta - p\cos\theta\right)\sin\theta}{p}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0

\ddot{\phi} + \dfrac{\left(\partial_\phi p\,\partial_u p - p\,\partial_u\partial_\phi p\right)\csc^2\theta}{r}\dot{u}^2 - \dfrac{2\partial_u p}{p}\dot{u}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{2}{r}\dot{r}\dot{\phi} + \dfrac{\partial_\phi p\,\csc^2\theta}{p}\dot{\theta}^2 + \dfrac{2\left(p\cos\theta - \partial_\theta p\,\sin\theta\right)\csc\theta}{p}\dot{\theta}\dot{\phi} - \dfrac{\partial_\phi p}{p}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
